When I was about 15, alone in the flat one afternoon, I sneaked into my mother’s writing desk and found a small pocket calendar from 1946 pushed to the back of a drawer. I had grown up with my mother and her parents, not knowing who my biological father was, or how I had come about; the question was simply never asked. I turned, with a kind of dread, to the entries from nine months before I was born. In mid-March there was an ordinary note – ‘Party at the Academic Association’; she was training as a laboratory technician in Lund and liked the students’ company – and on the following day, in her hand, five words: ‘God, what have I done!’ I still remember the shock of standing there with the diary, half-guilty for trespassing on her private papers, and saying aloud, over and over: ‘That’s me – that’s me. What have you done? I’m a mistake.’

For half a century, the scene stayed as it was: fixed, private, finished. Then, about a decade ago, I posted it – to several hundred old acquaintances and strangers – on Facebook. I was in doubt; I felt faint embarrassment at making it public, but this was itself part of what I wanted to examine. Why was it shameful? What did the shame tell me about myself? And would saying it out loud, to strangers, do anything to drain the memory of its sting? The answers came from my readers, and one of them showed me something I could not have seen on my own.

Betty, a friend from the years we were postdocs together at Stanford, had heard me tell the story in person long ago, and she said the written version was missing something: my voice, the intonation and the look on my face. What look, I asked – had I played it for sympathy, had I ironised it? ‘Absolutely flat,’ she wrote. ‘No affect. A Max von Sydow deadpan. But yes, you ironised.’ I had not known that about myself: that I’d delivered the central wound of my origins with no expression at all and turned it into a dry joke.

That discovery, prompted by a reader’s response, was one of the first signs that writing one’s life in public could change how memory and narrative take shape. Writing an autobiography or memoir was traditionally a solitary undertaking. Authors worked through papers, memories and past events largely on their own, occasionally consulting family, friends or colleagues. Only after years of private work would the manuscript reach the public. Readers encountered the finished account, with little sense of the revisions, doubts and shifts in understanding that had shaped it.

Social media has fundamentally disrupted these conditions. By publishing sequential episodes of my life every few days, however, I have turned my autobiographical drafts into a continuing dialogue with my readers. Their real-time responses have made me reconsider how I understand my professional achievements, my personal relationships and myself. The question that drives it is not what happens when you put a memoir on Facebook, but a quieter one: what happens to self-image when it is formed in public?

As a professional historian of science, I have always been fascinated by biographies, autobiographies and memoirs – viewing them not merely as raw material for writing history, or even microhistories, but as distinct accounts of the past in their own right. Yet now, writing my life story piece by piece in public, I’ve begun to question whether a life can ever be framed, genuinely, as a coherent narrative – and whether that uncertainty might be a good thing.
I chose to focus on the personal context, developing an approach I termed existential scientific biography

I first tried my hand at full-scale life-writing in 1986, shortly after I finished my first book, on the history of Swedish ecology. Almost accidentally, I met with Niels Kaj Jerne, the Danish immunologist who had been awarded the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine just two years earlier. ‘I have saved some papers,’ he casually remarked as we sat talking over a glass of wine in the kitchen of his large villa in southern France. We went up to the spacious attic room, where he parted the shutters and gestured towards the ancient Roman aqueduct, the Pont du Gard. Yet, I had no interest in antiquity; my attention was entirely arrested by the hundreds of grocery bags from the local supermarché lined up across the stone floor. They were stuffed to the brim with intimate letters, private diaries, raw laboratory protocols, rough article drafts, and decades of correspondence with colleagues around the world. He had kept virtually every scrap of paper that had passed through his hands from his youth onwards.

I can still vividly recall the thrill of exploring this unique archive. That afternoon set in motion a seven-year cooperation. At the outset, we discussed the possibility of weaving biography and autobiography together; we toyed with the idea of a book in a parallel format, with my biographical text on the left-hand pages and his personal recollections on the right – auto/biography as interlocution.

The vision of a side-by-side account soon faded, however, because Jerne – who was then in his mid-70s – lacked the stamina to draft his own memoir. Instead, through hundreds of hours of conversation, I managed to elicit a wealth of memory fragments that continuously enriched, and occasionally disrupted, my developing account of him.

Jerne’s unusual candour about his personal and intimate life led me, early on, to view his private and scientific realms as an integrated whole. Most of my colleagues in the history of science viewed biography as an ancilla historiae – a handmaid to history – and thus focused on the social and cultural context of researchers and their work. In contrast, I chose to focus on the personal context, developing an approach I termed existential scientific biography. As a lifelong admirer of Søren Kierkegaard, Jerne enthusiastically embraced this framework.

Jerne died in 1994. By the time my book about him, Science as Autobiography, appeared in 2003, I had been appointed professor of the history of medicine at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark. There, I hoped to focus on medical biography and autobiography. But I quickly became absorbed in transforming the university’s medical history museum into Medical Museion. My life-writing went on standby for several years.

It was only upon retiring 10 years ago that I found myself free to resume my fascination with life-writing, now with the roles reversed: after decades spent writing the lives of others, I would become my own subject. The decision was sparked one afternoon while I was clearing out my office at the museum. I suddenly realised how much material I had accumulated without having given it a second thought while I lived my life ‘forwards’, as Kierkegaard once put it.

My almost 50-year-long academic paper trail was a cornucopia of manuscripts, bundles of correspondence, lecture notes, meeting minutes and calendars. These were not in shopping bags on a stone floor, but in magazine files and stacks on office shelves. Yet the emotional impulse was the same as in Jerne’s attic room in Languedoc 30 years earlier, and I was seized by an irresistible urge to reconstruct my own life. It was high time to begin understanding life ‘backwards’. I was about to turn 70 and I realised – much like Socrates – that the unexamined life is not worth living. What had I achieved? How had I used my talents, and what mistakes had I made? Could I go to my grave without answering such questions?

Who, besides myself, could be interested in the answers? Unlike Jerne, I was not a well-known figure – but that was, paradoxically, a virtue. For me, the examined life mattered as a souci de soi, an act of self-care. I thought of the writing exercise as a present-day, healthy ageing counterpart to the late-medieval and early modern ars moriendi – the art of dying well.
I spent three years reading and taking notes, year by year, page by page

And for others, I thought, my autobiography might be of interest as an experiment and an example: I wanted my readers to focus on questions of genre without being distracted by the historical (in)significance of the subject.

I packed the professional papers into removal boxes and set up an archive room in the basement at home, adding my private papers – school essays, diaries, personal letters and photographs – and also downloaded tens of thousands of work-related files and emails from the university server. I then spent three years reading and taking notes, year by year, page by page. Much was factual and emotionally neutral. Some old articles stirred a sense of pride; others were downright embarrassing. Angry letters from former intimate partners were particularly painful to revisit.

The emotional rollercoaster had its counterpart in the labour of memory. I would lie on the bed with the curtains drawn and earplugs in, to stifle sensory impressions, transporting myself in imagination to the many places I had lived, visited and worked, and the people I had met, trying to capture my immediate feelings of pleasure, joy, longing, unease, sorrow or fear as I recalled them. These deliberately summoned memories were then supplemented by the thousands of fragments that surfaced as I worked my way through the archive.

Archival documents and memories are the obvious source materials for anyone writing their autobiography – and gathering them had so far been exactly the solitary labour the genre is known for: the lone author behind drawn curtains, exhuming papers and interrogating memory. But few authors go further and seek out the people they have encountered throughout their lives. As an experienced oral historian – both for the history of ecology and, later, for the Jerne biography – I had already spent hundreds of hours interviewing others about their lives. So it was a natural step to turn the same method on myself, and supplement the archival records and my own memories by contacting people from my past – childhood and adolescent friends, schoolmates, teachers, former colleagues, and even former girlfriends – in order to flesh out and contrast my self-image with their perspectives. Some declined; others had little more than banalities to offer (‘you were tall and thin’), but many were surprisingly candid. Over the years, I have spoken with several hundred acquaintances and colleagues, and have renewed a couple of lost connections – though not romantic ones. These conversations were the first breach in the traditional solitude of the genre.

It was almost inevitable that my autobiography would be existential. I wanted to understand how my years as an academic researcher and teacher were interwoven with my life as a whole: upbringing and education, personality and aesthetic preferences, political and moral commitments, social and personal relationships. Inspired by the French philosopher Pierre Hadot, I conceived of my intellectual work as ‘a form of life’; I therefore regarded my archives, memories and conversations with friends, colleagues and acquaintances as ‘spiritual exercises’ that could help me towards greater self-awareness. In the words of Michel Foucault: as a ‘technology of the self’.

In addition to the existential approach, there was yet another aspect of life-writing that I brought with me from my experiences with Jerne, namely the cooperative construction of a life story. And what makes that construction possible, at scale and with readers, is the medium.

What is new in my project is the move onto social media. For me, this was no great leap: a decade before I began the memoir, I had begun blogging, and later Tweeting, extensively about the museum’s transformation. So, when I embarked on my autobiography, writing it on social media felt entirely natural.

I chose Facebook – it lends itself to longer texts, and it was where many of my old friends and colleagues were already. I posted several times a week: striking memories, interesting documents I had read, engaging conversations with old schoolmates, and, not least, spontaneous reflections on genre. I wrote in Swedish, my mother tongue, in my adopted Danish, and in English, as the mood took me. The posts formed a florilegium: a gathering of flowers in the original sense of the word. Gradually, I accumulated friends and followers, who began responding to the life I was putting before them. A dialogue was quietly getting under way.

After a few years of unstructured writing, I began to proceed systematically, still on Facebook, of course, but now in a feuilleton format – a serial form published in instalments. One might suppose that my inspiration was the serialised novel of the 19th century, but my actual model was not Dickens, Dostoevsky or Dumas; it was the dramaturgy of the television series: the division into seasons, the thematically coherent episodes, the tension between what is resolved and what is left open – and the cliffhanger.

I have provisionally divided the feuilleton into 16 seasons, from childhood to a final season about my autobiographical work and my second set of children. I do not write and publish them strictly chronologically, but in the order that satisfies my curiosity and nostalgic cravings. (Though once I have started a season, I see it through chronologically in its entirety before moving on to the next.)
I have no master plan telling me in advance which parts of my life will matter

An episode is a thematically coherent Facebook post of 300-500 words that takes a specific situation or experience as its point of departure. Working from a raw file of letters, diary entries and present-day reflections, I winnow the material and try to render what happened clearly enough for some meaning to emerge. Each episode must be able to stand alone, intelligible and engaging even for those who only occasionally follow my Facebook feed.

How many episodes a season holds emerges only in the writing, as readers’ comments spur new insights and new episodes. And above all, I have no master plan telling me in advance which parts of my life will matter.

An average episode takes roughly a day to formulate. I begin with a private draft written from my own authorial perspective, then copy-and-paste it to the Facebook text box and continue working, now with the reader’s gaze in mind. It is often only when writing the Facebook version that my inner reader discovers weaknesses that my inner author had overlooked – much as a writer catches in the proofs what they missed in the manuscript. Sometimes, the point of an episode only becomes clear just before I press ‘send’ at lunchtime and wait for the responses that come in throughout the afternoon and evening.
Working at this pace, I can publish three or four episodes a week; across the whole project, I have posted almost 2,000 times, serving up autobiography as soap opera.

The crucial difference between writing one’s autobiography in traditional book form and writing it as a feuilleton on social media is the possibility of entering into a dialogue with readers from the earliest stages. The profile currently has more than 1,000 followers from Sweden, Denmark, the UK and the US, and each post usually draws at least a handful of comments; occasionally as many as 200. Most responses come from a core group of around 100 regular participants; they come from every walk of life, and some of the sharpest remarks come from readers with no scholarly training at all. In recent years, however, this engagement has diminished, partly reflecting a general trend on social media, but perhaps also a waning interest in the project itself (another similarity with TV series).

The comments vary widely. Some followers recount similar experiences; others correct factual details or suggest literature for contextualising the episode; still others offer alternative interpretations. The best exchanges have the intensity and quality of a good seminar with a small group of students or colleagues. Like in-person seminars, I respond to every comment, often revising language that might give rise to misunderstanding.

No single exchange has been revolutionary; what matters is the accumulation – hundreds of small corrections and re-readings, settling slowly into a different sense of who I have been. I do not know what the next episode will look like, how the season will end, or what shape the whole will take.

The deepest corrections altered the account of the person I was. In the season about my years as a PhD student, I describe an event relating to a former partner, Lone. We had lived together in Copenhagen in the mid-1970s, but the relationship was troubled, as I remember it, because of her mood swings, which I attributed to her diabetes. I left her for someone else and then stopped thinking about her almost entirely. Years afterward, she suddenly wrote to me, saying she had been evicted from her flat and asked for help. I did not answer. On my 40th birthday, she sent me an envelope lined with red silk paper, empty inside. I did not answer that either. It was only when I began the memoir decades later that I searched for her in the Danish public registry and discovered she had died in her early 40s, alone as far as I could tell. I then remembered I had once promised her I would be there when she died and plant daisies on her grave, and felt guilty about not having fulfilled my pledge.

What the post did not give me, the readers did in their comments. An old neighbour, Eva, who had known Lone, supplied a fuller portrait than I had been able to manage on my own; I had been writing, I admitted to her in the comments, ‘under the influence of my memory of the bad aspects of the relationship’. Another reader, Barbro, caught me in a single line: people would describe her own personality much as I had described Lone’s, she wrote – and she had never had diabetes. I had inadvertently conflated Lone’s difficult personality with her chronic illness in a way that exonerated my decision to leave her. A third reader, Kristina, asked what I thought the empty envelope had meant. I tried to deflect: I had been blank then and was blank now. She refused the deflection – she had not asked what I thought back then, she had asked what I think now. When I still had no answer, she offered one: a beautiful container with nothing inside, a friendship promised for a lifetime that turned out to be air. The process was forcing the container open, allowing a small, late act of atonement when another reader, Carolina, suggested I plant the daisies anywhere beautiful, since I had no grave to find. But I have still not planted them.
I had to defend – or reconsider – my gaze in real time, under the scrutiny of people I respect

Readers are no gentler with my professional life than with my private one. Now and then, they puncture the version of myself I have just offered. In one post, I recounted an episode from the final year of my PhD studies, when I attended the Swedish annual meeting for historians of science. The morning’s keynote, by the most powerful professor in the field just back from a sabbatical at Berkeley, had struck me as a long and self-satisfied catalogue of the distinguished colleagues he had met and the dinners he had attended. My irritation grew with the square of the elapsed minutes. When the floor opened, I put up my hand and asked, with deliberate weight on the adjective and no softening preamble, whether he had got any intellectual benefit from his trip as well. There was a silence, then scattered tittering. The chairman immediately declared coffee break, and I felt like a king for a few minutes amid the other doctoral students’ admiration (‘How did you dare?’), until the keynote speaker’s own student looked at me with a dry smile and said: ‘There you’ve evidently destroyed your career in Swedish history of science.’ He was right; I took my future ambitions to Denmark.

I posted this as a cautionary anecdote, but some of my readers declined to let it stay one. One refused the heroic frame: I was not brave, Mats said, but rather ‘naive and insensitive’; I could have asked the same legitimate question in a way that sought an answer rather than an audience. I conceded: ‘Yes, it was provocative and foolhardy.’ An American colleague, Richard, turned the story over and read its underside – call it instead ‘How I began my career in Denmark’ – and I had to agree that leaving the Swedish history-of-science milieu was my intellectual salvation. My Danish colleague Jes moved the lens onto vanity itself: gracious answers existed that would have honoured the question without diminishing the questioner, but they require the one quality rarest in academic life, ‘the absence of a dominating vanity’ – and then he caught his own pretension in the act of saying so.

Between them, the three readers dislodged the small monument I had built to my own courage and showed me the vanity inside it. The thread also made me admit that this was not a single youthful lapse but a pattern: I had done the same to a leading European scholar a few years later.

Sometimes, the dialogue puts the act of telling itself on trial. I once posted a memory from a conference in the 1980s, dominated in my recollection by a young female doctoral student wearing a Mickey Mouse T-shirt that prominently accentuated her breasts – an image that, at the time, had prompted hushed, stereotypical jokes among the male attendees about ‘Mickey’s ears’. I described it as a moment in which she deliberately played on her gender.

The reaction from my Facebook readers was swift and polarised. A younger colleague attacked the post as sordid, accusing me of reproducing today the same objectifying male gaze I claimed merely to be reporting from the past. Another woman read the student’s choice as a breaching experiment – a conscious subversion of the grey academic dress code. A third defended my right to report the past as I remembered it, noting the ‘Lutheran asceticism’ often demanded of female academics, and offered her own counter-anecdote about a male presenter whose thin linen trousers had distracted an entire audience.

The dialogue did not correct my memory, but it forced me into an uncomfortable ethical confrontation with my own role as narrator. Was I documenting the past, or was I still looking through that same 1980s lens? The ethical practice lies in exactly this friction: the feuilleton format made it impossible to hide behind polished, retrospective wisdom. I had to defend – or reconsider – my gaze in real time, under the scrutiny of people I respect.

Lessons like these keep me drawn to the feuilleton format. My readers have helped to make these years of autobiographical writing the most absorbing, enjoyable and meaningful of my long academic life. To paraphrase Socrates again: the examined life, in dialogue with others, is truly worth living.

I recently scored very highly on the ‘openness’ scale in a Big Five personality test, which puts a psychological gloss on the entire project. The feuilleton format showed my preference for living with open questions and unresolved interpretations, rather than striving towards a finished account of my life.

My openness also had an intellectual precedent in my training as a historian of science. There, I had learned to distinguish between ‘ready-made science’ and ‘science in the making’, as Bruno Latour had put it. The lesson was not to build historical writing on published articles and textbooks alone, but to regard research as a provisional process through which facts are slowly assembled and stabilised.
I think of my autobiographical writing on social media as something similar. It is, in the most literal sense, an autobiography in the making.

Even so, when I began this project, I took it for granted that it would arrive somewhere – that the long labour of extracting from archives, summoning memories, and talking to others would eventually compose itself into a coherent narrative of my life.

This is a common conception of autobiography as a genre. The French autobiography scholar Philippe Lejeune holds that it is a retrospective prose narrative; within identity research, life stories are regarded as a fundamental form of self-understanding – the view being that we all live in and through stories about ourselves, and that a good life means shaping a unified life story. Narrativity is seen as a moral ideal: the good, examined life is, by definition, a narrated life.
Each episode must be readable on its own; the reader need not know everything that has preceded it

But there are dissenting voices. The British philosopher Galen Strawson distinguishes between those who experience themselves diachronically, as a single self unfolding through time, and those who understand themselves episodically. Such people experience their lives as a sequence of fragments rather than as a coherent whole, and yet can be fully reflective and morally serious. Strawson’s chief witness is Michel de Montaigne – perhaps the greatest autobiographer in world literature – who moves freely between fragments, paradoxes and unfinished reflections in an open-ended exploration that never resolves into a story.

I learned how stubborn the narrative assumption can be when I tried to enlist my readers on Strawson’s side. Scarcely a year into the project, I posted a link to his seminal article ‘Against Narrativity’ (2004), expecting nods of agreement. Instead, I got a quarrel that ran late into the night. One of my sharpest readers, Christian, objected that we are not one story but many small, situational ones. I held my ground: I knew my own past as a heap of fragments, not as a plotted tale. Only afterwards did I see what the argument had really been about. Christian was reading continuity and coherence into my life even as he denied doing any such thing.

Looking back at my own feuilleton, I realise I am closer to Strawson’s episodic self-understanding than to the retrospective narrative of classical autobiography. I did not begin with the vision of telling a story about myself: I began with the basement archive, the memory fragments and the conversations with friends. I bring out letters, diary entries, remembered images and the voices of others, trying to do justice to a situation, a mood, a conflict, a crossroads. Each episode must be readable on its own; the reader need not know everything that has preceded it, nor guess what is to come. If there is a Bildungsreise, it is full of detours, interruptions, dead-ends and retreats. If there is a moral, it is local and provisional – not a step in an overarching arc of personal development.

The form itself works against tidying. Because I publish short, self-contained episodes in rapid succession, it is difficult to reshape what I have written into a narrative without readers noticing; any attempt to harmonise the whole after the fact runs up against episodes already published. The open feuilleton thus becomes a safeguard against the kind of retrospective and self-flattering narrativity that Strawson warns against.

I once caught myself doing the very thing the open feuilleton is supposed to protect against – and the form saved me from myself. Something I had carried as private shame for most of my academic life was a compulsion to raise my hand at conferences and seminars. After one such meeting in 1979, I had written in my diary that, as usual, I could not restrain myself, giving in to a ‘pathological drive’ to dominate the room with my questions: ‘I am conditioned to the moment of questioning a speaker. I cannot keep my mouth shut. My heart pounds; I feel an irresistible compulsion … What is this inner need to show myself off in company?’ The pattern was unmistakable: wherever I sat – a hundred people in the room, time for only two questions – I had to ask one of them; I could count on my fingers the few occasions I managed simply to listen. And immediately afterwards, always, the shame: not at the behaviour, which was harmless enough, but at being unable to govern the impulse. I posted this and asked whether others knew the feeling. They did, and the thread ran long and serious into the afternoon, 90 comments in all.

What I had not noticed was that, in copying out the diary entry for the post, I had reduced five words to an ellipsis. That evening I went back to the original to see what the ellipsis had swallowed. The five elided words were: ‘compare Harry Belafonte on Arholma’. I knew at once what they meant. The summer I was 11, the only child in a roomful of adults at a guesthouse on the island of Arholma, a summer resort north of Stockholm, I had been coaxed into singing and had chosen Belafonte’s ‘Banana Boat Song’. A few shaky verses in, my great-uncle said, loudly, to the room: ‘Can’t someone shut that child up?’ The line had landed like a whiplash and lodged there.

The genuinely unsettling discovery was not the buried memory itself, but what I had done with it. I had, in fact, already written an episode connecting that humiliation, explicitly, to the seminar compulsion – and when I sat down to write about the compulsion the second time, I had forgotten the connection completely and even pruned the clue out of my own quotation. I posted the recovery the next day as what it plainly was: a specimen of forgetting, almost in a Freudian sense – that one can write about a painful thing in a detached, factual way and still keep mislaying it, precisely because it is too uncomfortable to hold. The form had caught me, in public and across two days, in the act of reading my own life badly – and only the second reading, prompted by the readers and by going back to the source, set it right.

I do not see this as a pessimistic conclusion, but as a liberating one. Strawson’s critique helps me calibrate my ambitions: to aim for fidelity to the fragments rather than the false comfort of a whole. If one thinks – as many narrativists do – that the essential task is to shape a unified self-narrative, the temptation is always there to smooth over ruptures, play down contradictions, and tidy away whatever doesn’t fit. The drive for narrative risks crowding out the unpredictable, the messy and the recalcitrant that make up much of our lived experience.
What I resist is not coherence but the imperative to impose it

The process matters far more to me than the result; even so, I have not ruled out publishing the final text as a book. But that intention sits uneasily with everything I have just argued: to edit the stream of episodes into a single volume risks imposing a coherence that was never there. Perhaps a narrative will emerge in the editing; perhaps it will not.

Autobiography, as I now practise it, is a series of soundings of how I relate to episodes from my life in light of today’s feelings, knowledge and relationships. What I resist is not coherence but the imperative to impose it.

This is also why I no longer regard autobiography as a final report on a life, in which questions such as ‘What have I achieved?’ or ‘What mistakes did I make?’ find definitive answers. The questions I now ask myself are different: how do I bear the consequences of what I have done? Which ties from the past do I wish to affirm, which must I accept, and which can, and should, I try to dissolve? The feuilleton has become a way of living with my past: testing my reactions against those of others, reconsidering my judgments, and trying out different descriptions of the same event.

When I return to Kierkegaard and Socrates, I do so with scepticism towards the self-image I held when I began packing my papers into removal boxes. To live forwards and understand it backwards need not mean capturing my life in a single narrative stream. It may be that I never finish understanding but continue to try – episode by episode.

Socrates’ reminder that the unexamined life is not worth living is too easily heard as a demand that the examined life be a well-told one. I would put it differently today: the too neatly narrated life risks becoming a poorly read one.

Dolly Parton’s estate says yellow caution tape and barbed wire crisscrossed the steps to her nephew Bryan Seaver’s front door as a process server was making repeated attempts to serve him with a lawsuit accusing him of using a “campaign of threats” to “extract money” from the late music icon’s business interests.

Lawyers for the estate filed a photo of the alleged barricade as they urged a judge to deny Seaver’s request for additional time to find a lawyer in the messy legal dispute. They also argued that Seaver’s security company missed a deadline last week to challenge an emergency restraining order granted in the case, so the order should therefore be converted into a permanent injunction covering both the company and Seaver himself, as its chief. A hearing on the matter is set for Friday, Oct. 9, unless the court grants Seaver’s request for more time to hire an attorney.

“Mr. Seaver attempted to evade service of process, and this court should not reward that behavior,” the estate’s lawyers wrote in their response filed Monday and obtained by Rolling Stone. They said the company that was set up to manage Parton’s estate after her death, called She’s Alive LLC, tried to serve Seaver on three occasions without success.

On one attempt, the process server observed four cars in the driveway, but no one answered at the front door, the new filing said. “Eventually, Mr. Seaver’s residence had a no-trespassing sign in the front yard and barbed wire draped across the handrails leading to the front door,” the filing alleged.

An attached photo appeared to show the barbed wire strung across the railings of Seaver’s five-step porch, tagged with strips of yellow caution tape and surrounded by a festive selection of pumpkins. Seaver did not respond to a request for comment asking if the display might have been part of his home’s Halloween decorations or potentially served some other purpose.

Seaver’s dispute with Danny Nozell, Parton’s longtime manager and the sole manager of She’s Alive LLC, first spilled into public view when Nozell sued him last month and sought the restraining order. Nozell accused Seaver of interfering with business relationships through “threats, intimidation, and coercion.” In granting the temporary restraining order ahead of the larger hearing, the judge cited a series of emails and other communications that she said appeared to pair “threats with demands for payment.”

Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles of Nashville Chancery Court ordered Seaver to remain 1,000 feet from estate employees and business partners, stay off private property controlled by the estate, and refrain from disruptive or harassing conduct.

Seaver is the relative who announced Parton’s Aug. 25 death in a video posted to her Instagram account, which drew millions of reactions. According to court filings, Seaver previously worked for private military contractors and later provided security for Parton and her properties through his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services (SAPS), which is also a party to the lawsuit.
In several messages quoted in the ruling, Seaver allegedly threatened Nozell and other people connected to Parton’s estate.
“I’m going to destroy the entire brand if you don’t get these [Dollywood business partners] out of our bit,” Seaver allegedly wrote on Aug. 19, about a week before Parton’s death at age 80.

After Parton died, Seaver purportedly wrote in another message: “I just sold 29 million dollars worth of ammo to Haiti. I’m not exactly a media person, Danny. I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary.”

Myles wrote that the statements were significant “not merely because of their language in isolation,” but because they accompanied threats directed at specific people and business interests. She cited one message in which Seaver purportedly threatened to start a podcast devoted to damaging Parton’s brand partnerships unless he was compensated. Myles said Seaver also made statements that invoked “his claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate.”

Seaver was removed from his security role connected to Parton’s business on Sept. 15, according to a letter from lawyers for She’s Alive filed in the case. The letter, obtained by Rolling Stone, said the termination did not affect Seaver’s separate interest as a beneficiary of the trust.

“The co-trustees will be in contact with you and the other beneficiaries in the near future regarding your interest as a beneficiary of the Trust,” the letter said. “All parties hope that this will be a smooth transition, and the trust group looks forward to corresponding with you as one of the beneficiaries.”

Myles said Seaver had until Friday, Oct. 2, to respond if he intended to contest the restraining order. When the deadline hit, Seaver asked the court for more time, saying he had “immediately” begun searching for a lawyer after being served but that his “preferred attorney” was not available to meet with him until Monday, Oct. 5.
Lawyers for the estate countered Monday that SAPS, as a corporate defendant, could not represent itself and was required to appear through a lawyer. The judge did not immediately issue a ruling.

In an earlier statement to TMZ, Seaver defended his messages to Nozell, saying they had been taken out of context. “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments,” he said. “However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”

Throughout the summer of 2026, there were plenty of signs of what was to come. Every week, it seemed, artificial intelligence models were offering proofs of decades-old mathematical conjectures. So what happened on September 8 shouldn’t have been a complete surprise. And yet to many it felt sudden, almost violent. OpenAI announced that its models had solved one of math’s most famous problems — and immediately sparked a controversy over authorship and standards. Mathematics would never be the same.

“In whatever years I have left, I don’t expect that I’ll ever again prove a theorem because I’m actually needed to prove it,” Scott Aaronson of the University of Texas, Austin wrote on his blog. “Human mathematicians are forevermore dethroned as the main theorem-proving entities on planet earth.” Other online missives expressed optimism, but many revealed some combination of grief, confusion, and fear.

Two days after the announcement, I found myself in a classroom at the University of California, Berkeley, surrounded by some 150 students, postdocs, and professors. The mathematician Ken Ono, who left academia for an AI start-up called Axiom Math, was scheduled to give a talk. “You might be graduating into a profession that might not even exist, or that will be very different than what you expected,” Ono told them. “You need to brace.”

The audience responded with anger and frustration. There were whispers and exchanged glances; Ono couldn’t make it through a single slide without a fresh wave of questions. “I’m not entirely sure what our takeaway is supposed to be,” one student said. Another asked how Ono and his start-up would take responsibility in light of “the shameful way that AI companies are treating mathematics.”

When Ono said that mathematicians would do their “very best” to avoid the bleak future the students were envisioning, a third retorted, hands trembling: “What are you doing? What is your ‘very best’?” The talk, including time for questions, had been allotted 50 minutes; with the extended Q&A, it went on for more than two hours. Many students lingered afterward, to vent and console one another.

To me, the reasons for these emotional reactions were obvious. The young mathematicians recognized that their field would have to change or risk extinction. What did surprise me was that when I returned to New York and brought it up in conversations with friends or family, they didn’t see what the problem was. All sorts of amazing discoveries are around the corner, they imagined. Wasn’t that the point?

These conversations exposed a long-standing problem: Many people don’t know what mathematics really is, or why mathematicians do it. Now mathematicians need to answer that question for themselves and explain it to the rest of the world — quickly. How they answer will determine what happens next.

As an undergraduate, I studied both mathematics and literature. I always found that “pure math” — the study of mathematical concepts for their own sake, without a care for real-world applications — existed somewhere between the sciences and the arts. It prizes logic and certainty, but at its core lie fuzzier notions of beauty, intuition, and depth. “Math is either the most science-y humanities or the most humanities-type science, depending who you ask,” said Marcel Goh, a doctoral student at McGill University. Usually it’s utterly useless, yet time and again its abstractions demonstrate “unreasonable effectiveness” in applications to physics and beyond.

In mathematics, it’s not a cliché that the journey matters more than the destination. Problems are posed not so much because their answers will be practical and important, but because they represent interesting journeys. The hope is that as mathematicians struggle to solve a problem, they’ll come up with intriguing tools and connections, stumble on novel ideas and directions, take fruitful detours, and answer new questions they never would have thought to ask.

“It was never about the theorems,” Goh said. “It’s to carry on a tradition that has benefited society despite not having any market value. To reason deeply, to understand the world … and to spread that knowledge.”

AI models skip to the end. At the moment, their proofs are nearly impossible to read. They elide salient details and waste pages on irrelevant concepts. They fail to demonstrate how the new work builds on or connects to other results in the mathematical literature. Mathematicians know that the proofs are true — they’re verified by a system that checks their logic — but have no idea why. What’s missing is understanding, the currency that mathematicians trade in. If there is a journey, humans are not invited along for the ride.

It’s as if you were teleported to the peak of a tall mountain. Surrounded by fog, you have no idea where you are, or what’s around you. You do not know how your mountain connects to others, and you have no equipment to help you explore, no way to help someone else join you. If you had climbed the mountain yourself, you would have experienced how the human body adapts to altitude and changes in oxygen levels. You might have had to invent tools to navigate, to climb steep cliffs, or to make a shelter. You might have encountered a fellow explorer, gotten lost together in a hidden valley, and found a plant that could be turned into a life-saving medicine.
Instead you’re perched on the peak but in the dark, while the maker of the teleportation machine tells you that it can explore the wilderness better than any human.
Mathematicians have always known that understanding is more valuable than an answer. So why should an AI answer machine feel like such a threat?

In part, it’s because of the way mathematics has evolved. For centuries, proving theorems and understanding those proofs have gone hand in hand. If someone solves a problem that the mathematical community has decided is central and important and hard, that solution is considered a reflection of deep insight and creativity.

So mathematical culture has developed almost entirely around problem-solving. Graduate students cut their teeth on simpler versions of big, complex problems, then seek to get their work published, find good jobs, and earn credit and recognition — all of which are assessed in terms of the theorems they prove. The incentive structures that power the mathematical community are not set up for a world where solving problems is easy and understanding their answers remains hard. “It breaks our system,” said Tasmin Chu, a doctoral student at the California Institute of Technology. “It just takes it to its absolute limit and destroys it.”
Over the past few months, I’ve heard from lots of mathematicians, students and senior researchers alike, about the shape of this destruction.

Companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic are competing directly against mathematicians (and poaching many of them) to quickly prove theorems, while putting little effort into writing clear papers to explain those results or put them in context. Most mathematicians have no idea what these companies have even proved at this point; OpenAI has announced that it’s keeping more than 100 important results secret. (This has the further effect of discouraging mathematicians from working on questions that might already be moot.)

“What is happening is a huge damage to open science,” Chu said. The only possible value of this is shareholder value. It completely overlooks the central mathematical enterprise — and, even worse, it seeks to overwrite it.

Many mathematicians have stopped posting open conjectures and potential ideas at the end of their papers, for fear that they’ll be scraped by bots and fed into AI models. Others are posting their papers before they’re ready in order to avoid getting scooped. Journals and the online preprint server arxiv.org have been overrun with AI-assisted or AI-generated proofs that no one can properly digest or check, which forces researchers to do the hard, currently thankless work of rewriting the proofs so they can actually benefit the mathematical community. (Even as models improve and those papers get easier to read, their sheer volume will overwhelm current systems for sorting through new work and deciding what’s interesting and important. In the meantime, arxiv.org has started limiting authors to two submissions per month.) When an editor of Transactions on Machine Learning Research reached out to the authors of 10 papers slated for rejection, most either did not respond or could not answer basic questions about work they’d claimed as their own.

At the same time, MathOverflow, an online forum where mathematicians answer each other’s questions — connecting famous researchers with young students and leaving years of exchanges for future generations to read and learn from — is seeing a massive decline in activity, as students privately ask AI models their questions. Others don’t want to share ideas in another space exposed to bots.

The situation is heartbreaking. Part of what is so wonderful about mathematics is its open and honest collaboration, and its independence from political or corporate concerns. That’s not to say that there haven’t been other problems with the culture of mathematics — inequity and lack of access, among other things — but what’s special about that culture is at great risk without a signal change in the field’s incentive structure.
“The existing equilibrium has broken,” said Daniel Litt, a mathematician at the University of Toronto. “We’ll have to find a new one.”
There’s a range of possible futures based on how mathematicians collectively respond — or don’t respond — to this moment.

In one, “once the profession turns over, you have a collection of mathematicians who are trained in pushing a button without reading the outputs,” Litt said, rather than being trained to ask interesting questions and engage with the results. “There’s a bad future where if we don’t adapt, there’s just no more math in 50 years. No one is doing it, not even the machines.
“I’m not saying it’s likely,” he continued. “We’re not going to sleepwalk into that. But I think the world where we change nothing probably looks like that.”

There is a more optimistic alternative — assuming a new incentive structure that disengages problem-solving and theorem-proving from jobs, advancement, and recognition. “Mathematicians will be spending less time trying to peck on the permafrost, getting out mathematical gems with great effort,” said Pavel Etingof of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “They’ll be sourcing that kind of pecking more to AI and trying to interpret and understand and learn the results that will come from that. There will be a lot more mathematics to make sense of. And there will be a lot of work for mathematicians — maybe different work from before, but definitely interesting work.”

That work will involve, to some extent, studying proofs written by AI — the way every undergraduate learns the known proofs in their textbooks. Many mathematicians expect AI-generated arguments to graduate from slop to more elegant writing soon enough; perhaps within a few years, Litt said, “we’re reading beautifully written expositions of highly interesting results. To me, that’s the dream. That’s why I got into it.”

These future mathematicians will have much to do. After all, Litt added, “there’s no amount of well-writtenness that lets you understand math.” They’ll have to rewrite AI proofs, find more elegant arguments, come up with theories and frameworks and definitions, ask questions, formulate new conjectures, develop a sense of what’s interesting and important. They’ll be the ones building research programs, creating communities around certain ideas, and passing that knowledge on to others. (I am reminded of the literary theorist Roland Barthes’ famous 1967 essay “The Death of the Author,” in which he argues that it is the reader, and not the writer, who has ultimate control and agency in actively creating a work’s meaning.)

“If AI proves all possible theorems, and no mathematicians know about these theorems, it cannot be part of culture, because culture is inherently human,” Etingof said. “Those papers will only become a part of mathematical culture when some human reads them and understands them and gets something out of them.”
The question is whether the next generation of mathematicians will want to. Or even be able to.

Mathematicians are already rethinking how they’ll train their students, accept papers for publication (they’re currently experimenting with requiring accompanying talks), and make hiring decisions. There aren’t easy answers for more nebulous skills such as understanding, communication, and vision. But the stakes are high enough that I think they’ll succeed.
I’m less certain about whether new generations of mathematicians will be attracted to this remade discipline.

Many people are drawn to math because they want to solve problems, explore frontiers, and be the first to discover some new truth. Will they be willing to put in decades of training for the job of interpreter? They’ll still read and translate proofs and expect to rewrite them. But it seems less likely that they will frequently experience the same moments of clarity or sense of creative ownership.

“A lot of the reason why people do pure math, even though it pays so much less than industry, is because you get to author your own creative contributions and then give them to a community that appreciates them for their intellectual beauty,” Chu said. “This environment where mathematical discourse is centered around machines talking and humans listening, I don’t think it’s a very attractive one.”

And AI is itself undermining the kind of education that would be necessary for that role. This came up at the Berkeley colloquium, too. “There’s a serious risk that 20, 30, 40 years from now, there will be no people around who have the same classical mathematics training,” one student said. “I’m worried about a world where the full body of mathematical knowledge is inaccessible.”

The result could be a lost generation. Goh is one of many young mathematicians struggling with the angst such a future is producing, and with what he sees as a lack of effort on the part of working mathematicians (at least until very recently) to remake the incentives to avoid it.
“There’s something sick about the culture,” he told me. “I didn’t think so, but now I do.”

Goh is alarmed by how some have taken up AI without enough critical thought, and he feels pressured to use it so that he doesn’t get left behind. “I was just very depressed about that,” he said. “That doesn’t feel inspiring to me. … It didn’t have to be this way.”

He likens it to Saruman from The Lord of the Rings, corrupted by the promise of unlimited knowledge and power. Goh and a growing number of mathematicians are starting to consider themselves AI “vegetarians,” consciously measured in their use of the technology. There’s nothing rewarding or interesting or fun about offloading their cognition to a machine, they argue.
Goh is determined and would rather leave the field than use AI in his creative work. “I think the ship is sinking,” he admitted, “but I’ve already made my decision to stay on board as long as I can.”

There is, through all of this, reason for hope. Mathematicians see these problems and feel a collective sense of concern (if not panic), so they are working now to create attractive conditions for people in their field — both those interested in using AI and those who don’t want to. Chu and others have formed the Association for Human Mathematics, for example, because “what we need right now actually is not more mathematics but policy proposals and tools … to deal with this crisis and change our ecosystem.”

It will be hard. Inertia is powerful. But mathematics could come out of this stronger than before. Forced to name and prioritize what people love and value about the field, current and future mathematicians can emphasize skills that have previously been deprioritized: the ability to communicate and share knowledge, to develop a broad vision, to experiment with original ideas without feeling the need to publish theorem after theorem. To think deeply.

“I think there is a good future where we come out way ahead of where we are now, where we learn a huge amount of interesting math,” Litt said. “We have people doing the coolest stuff they’ve ever done. We have a really vibrant community of people who deeply understand stuff.”
If we can’t adapt, he added, “whose fault is that?”
Editor’s note: Scott Aaronson is a member of Quanta Magazine’s advisory board.
Scientists reveal what seven days of fasting does to the human body

- Scientists found that prolonged fasting triggers major changes throughout the body, but many of the most interesting effects only appeared after about three days without food. The results suggest fasting may influence health in ways that go beyond weight loss and could eventually inspire treatments that mimic its effects.

Going without food for several days does far more than force the body to burn stored fat. Research published in 2024 found that prolonged fasting produces widespread and coordinated biological changes across multiple organs, with some of the most notable effects appearing only after about three days without calories.

The findings, published in Nature Metabolism, offer an unusually detailed look at how the human body responds during an extended fast. Researchers found evidence of biological effects that went beyond weight loss, although many of the potentially health related changes did not become apparent until participants had gone roughly three days without food.

Scientists from Queen Mary University of London's Precision Healthcare University Research Institute (PHURI) and the Norwegian School of Sports Sciences conducted the work. By identifying the molecular changes associated with fasting, the researchers hope to provide a foundation for future studies that could eventually lead to treatments capable of reproducing some of fasting's effects.

That could be especially important for people who might benefit from certain biological effects of fasting but cannot safely undergo a prolonged fast or follow fasting mimicking approaches such as ketogenic diets.

Humans have evolved to tolerate extended periods without food, an ability that was essential during times when meals were unpredictable. Today, millions of people fast for cultural, religious, medical, or weight loss purposes.
Fasting also has a long history in medicine. It has been used in various forms to help manage conditions including epilepsy and rheumatoid arthritis.

One of the clearest changes during fasting involves the body's energy supply. Under normal conditions, much of the body's readily available energy comes from glucose derived from food. Once that incoming energy disappears, the body gradually begins drawing more heavily on stored fat.

Scientists already understood that basic metabolic shift. What has been much less clear is what prolonged fasting does throughout the rest of the body, including whether it produces biological changes that could be beneficial, harmful, or both (beneficial or adverse).

Modern protein analysis has made it possible to investigate those questions in far greater detail. Proteins carry out an enormous range of jobs in the body, from building tissues to controlling chemical reactions and transmitting signals between cells. Measuring thousands of proteins in the bloodstream can therefore provide a broad picture of how different organs and biological systems are responding.
For the study, researchers followed 12 healthy volunteers who completed a seven-day water-only fast.
Participants were closely monitored each day. The scientists measured changes in about 3,000 proteins in their blood before the fast, throughout the fasting period, and after they began eating again.

The researchers then combined those protein measurements with genetic information from large population studies. This allowed them to investigate which biological pathways were changing during fasting and to predict some of the possible health consequences associated with those changes.
As expected, the body began shifting away from glucose and toward stored fat as a major energy source during the first two or three days without food.

Participants lost an average of 5.7 kilograms during the fast, with the loss coming from both fat mass and lean mass. Lean mass includes tissues that are not body fat, such as muscle and other water-rich tissues.
Three days after participants resumed eating, their overall weight remained below where it had started. However, most of the lost lean mass had returned, while the reduction in fat mass remained.
The most striking finding involved what happened after approximately three days of fasting.

At that point, researchers began detecting distinct changes in the levels of proteins throughout the body. The pattern suggested that complete calorie restriction was producing a coordinated whole body response rather than simply altering how the body obtained energy.
About one third of all the proteins measured changed significantly during the fasting period, with effects linked to all major organs.
Many of those changes appeared consistently among the participants. The researchers also detected biological signatures that could not be explained by weight loss alone.

One example involved changes in proteins associated with the structural support of neurons in the brain. Neurons are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the nervous system, and the proteins surrounding and supporting them help maintain their structure and function.
The results suggest that prolonged fasting may influence a much wider range of biological processes than simply fat metabolism.
Potential Benefits Extend Beyond Weight Loss
Claudia Langenberg, Director of Queen Mary's Precision Health University Research Institute (PHURI), said:

"For the first time, we're able to see what's happening on a molecular level across the body when we fast. Fasting, when done safely, is an effective weight loss intervention. Popular diets that incorporate fasting - such as intermittent fasting - claim to have health benefits beyond weight loss. Our results provide evidence for the health benefits of fasting beyond weight loss, but these were only visible after three days of total caloric restriction - later than we previously thought."

The timing is important. Intermittent fasting can involve much shorter periods without food, while this study examined complete calorie restriction lasting several days. The results therefore do not mean that shorter fasting schedules necessarily produce the same effects.
Instead, the study helps identify when some of the more substantial molecular responses to prolonged fasting begin to appear.
Could Scientists Reproduce Fasting's Effects?
Understanding why fasting produces particular biological changes could eventually prove more important than fasting itself.

If researchers can determine which molecular pathways are responsible for potentially beneficial effects, it may become possible to develop treatments that activate those pathways without requiring patients to stop eating for several days.
That possibility could be especially useful for people whose medical conditions make prolonged fasting impractical or unsafe.
Maik Pietzner, Health Data Chair of PHURI and co-lead of the Computational Medicine Group at Berlin Institute of Health at Charité, said:

"Our findings have provided a basis for some age-old knowledge as to why fasting is used for certain conditions. While fasting may be beneficial for treating some conditions, often times, fasting won't be an option to patients suffering from ill health. We hope that these findings can provide information about why fasting is beneficial in certain cases, which can then be used to develop treatments that patients are able to do."

The study provides a detailed molecular map of how the human body adapts during prolonged fasting. It also highlights a notable threshold: while the switch toward burning stored fat begins within the first few days, many of the broader biological changes associated with fasting become detectable only after about three days without calories.

That distinction could help researchers separate the effects of weight loss from the deeper biological responses triggered by extended fasting, while providing new clues about how those responses might someday be reproduced without requiring people to undergo prolonged periods without food.

Dennis Hastert, longtime Republican House speaker who went to prison, dies at age 84

Dennis Hastert, whose political legacy as Congress' longest-serving Republican House speaker was later fouled by allegations that he had molested high school athletes during his prior career as a teacher and wrestling coach, has died, a coroner said Monday. He was 84.
Hastert, who was speaker from 1999 until 2007, died Saturday of natural causes at his home while receiving hospice care, according to Kendall County Coroner Jacquie Purcell.
When he was sentenced in 2016 to more than a year behind bars, the former history teacher became one of the highest-ranking American politicians ever ordered to prison.

In the late 1990s, Hastert was a little-known Illinois lawmaker with a reputation for congeniality that had helped him ascend the ranks of congressional leaders. When Newt Gingrich lost support because of ethics violations and the GOP's poor showing in an election, Republicans elected Hastert to succeed him. In his first weeks on the job, he presided over the House while the Senate conducted then-President Bill Clinton's impeachment trial.

After the GOP reclaimed the White House, Hastert helped pass then-President George W. Bush's legislative agenda, including massive tax cuts and a measure that amounted to a huge expansion of prescription drug benefits — the biggest change in Medicare in decades.

His legacy was suddenly thrown into doubt in 2015, when he was accused of evading banking regulations as part of a plan to pay hush money to conceal unspecified "prior misconduct." Nearly a year later, prosecutors filed papers that described what media reports had suggested for months: Hastert's alleged misconduct involved the sexual abuse of teenage boys on his wrestling team in the small town of Yorkville, west of Chicago.

During a 16-year coaching career, he led his team to a state championship and was named national coach of the year in 1976. But behind the accolades, prosecutors said, Hastert sexually abused at least four team members from 1965 to 1981.

The person Hastert was paying, identified in court papers only as Individual A, said the abuse occurred in a motel room when he was 14 on the way home from wrestling camp. Hastert allegedly touched other wrestlers in a locker room after saying he would give them massages. Two wrestlers said Hastert performed sexual acts on them.
Prosecutors also described a recliner where Hastert often sat in the locker room with a direct view of the stalls where the boys showered.
Hastert agreed to plead guilty to evading banking laws. In all, he paid more than $1.7 million out of $3.5 million that he had promised to Individual A, sometimes in lump sums of $100,000 cash.

At the sentencing hearing where he received 15 months behind bars, the visibly angry judge called Hastert a "serial child molester." A former wrestler struggled with his emotions as he told the court about his "dark secret" from adolescence.
In his own statement, Hastert said he was "deeply ashamed" and admitted that he "mistreated" some of his athletes. But he never referred directly to sexual abuse.
The public knew nothing about Hastert's past when Republicans lost seats in the 1998 midterm elections.

Hastert's path to the speaker's office was cleared when Louisiana Rep. Bob Livingston, who was considered a lock to replace Gingrich as speaker, resigned after acknowledging several extramarital affairs.
Hastert was aware of the personal pitfalls of holding the powerful position.

"You know, in this business, especially in a job like this, you can get your head someplace where it shouldn't be," Hastert said in a 1999 interview with The Associated Press. "But you come back home, and you're home. You're back where you've always been, and your feet are back on the ground."
Hastert said he lacked the appetite for higher office.
As the recount of the 2000 presidential election dragged on, Hastert's aides briefed him on the possibility that he might become acting president in the event of an Electoral College deadlock.

"I really didn't want to be president, temporary or otherwise," he wrote in his book. But he decided that he would not pass the office to the constitutional officer next in line if an Electoral College deadlock extended beyond Inauguration Day. In the end, the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling ended the recount, and Bush moved into the White House.
Hastert's journey to Congress from his boyhood farm appeared to be the result of fate and luck.

In 1980, he finished third in an Illinois House primary. But the incumbent became fatally ill, and GOP leaders chose Hastert to take his place on the November ballot, where he won in a traditional GOP stronghold.
Hastert became a congressional candidate in 1986 and beat the Democrat with 52% of the vote, his smallest margin of victory in a congressional race.
In Washington, Hastert served quietly in House leadership, working closely with Gingrich and then-House Majority Whip Tom DeLay after Republicans took control in 1995.
Hastert became wealthy largely through a complex web of transactions that coincided with one of his own highway earmarks increasing the value of land he had purchased in his district.
He was forced to step down as speaker in 2007, when Democrats gained control of the House, and he resigned his seat later that year.
Born in Aurora, Illinois, Hastert earned a bachelor's degree in economics from Wheaton College in 1964 and a master's in education from Northern Illinois University in 1967.

In 2007, Wheaton named its newly created public policy center the J. Dennis Hastert Center for Economics, Government and Public Policy. After Hastert's indictment, the school removed his name in 2015. Other organizations abandoned associations with Hastert, and his portrait was removed from a hallway outside the House chamber.
Hastert lived his entire life in Chicago's suburbs, primarily in the Yorkville area. While growing up, he helped his father with the family feed business.
Survivors include his wife, Jean, and two adult sons.

On Friday morning, Shivon Zilis, a top executive and lieutenant of Elon Musk at his brain chip implant company Neuralink—as well as mother of four of the 14 children he is known to have fathered—took to his social media platform, X, to announce an abrupt shift in their relationship.

“It’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week with no warning, but that’s just how it is sometimes,” Zilis wrote, sharing a screenshot of the X account @BigTechAlert that showed Musk had unfollowed her there. Zilis’ post continued: “I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,” followed by warm praise and best wishes for Musk. “I do hope and pray he and I can be great friends and coparents,” Zilis concluded, leaving some ambiguity as to what exactly changed between them and whether she remains a director of operations and special projects at Neuralink, though it does not appear as if she has left the position.

While this was a strange revelation of a private matter, it seemed hardly out of the ordinary for Musk’s dizzyingly complicated family life. At this point, all four of the women confirmed to have had children with him—Zilis, ex-wife Justine Wilson, Claire Boucher (better known as Grimes), and Ashley St. Clair—have used X to share details of their time with him or push back against his own claims.

Both Wilson and St. Clair participated in filmmaker Alex Gibney’s sprawling new documentary Musk, in theaters nationwide on October 16 and screening at the WIRED World Fair in Miami next month. St. Clair, a former conservative influencer, alleges that she rejected a nondisclosure agreement worth $40 million that would have prevented her from talking about her tumultuous association with Musk. Among an ensemble of tech entrepreneurs, journalists, and former Musk employees, the pair stand out as arguably the most important critical voices in the film, shedding light on Musk’s rise in Silicon Valley as well as his turn toward MAGA extremism during the 2024 election.

At a run time of nearly four hours, Musk sounds like daunting viewing, though once it’s over, you’ll find yourself wondering if it could’ve been a 10-part miniseries. That’s how much ground there is to cover, from the unrealistic ambitions of landing on Mars and the corporate colonization of Texas to the fatal collisions involving “self-driving” Teslas and the annihilation of the US Agency for International Development by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) at the beginning of Trump’s second term. (WIRED’s reporting is cited in the documentary, which features interviews with global editorial director Katie Drummond and contributing editor Zoë Schiffer.)

Alongside a fast-moving, comprehensive account of Musk’s career as an all-powerful and untouchable oligarch, his former romantic partners provide crucial context about exactly who he is, piecing together a devastating portrait of the type of man to “let go” of a significant other by unfollowing her on social media.

Wilson reflects movingly on the loss of their firstborn to a SIDS-related condition, which is juxtaposed with a Musk post on X in which he wrote that he held their infant son as he died—a comment to which his ex-wife replied, “not that it matters to anyone except me, because it is one of the most sacred and defining moments of my life, but I was the one who was holding him.”

In the film, she also addresses the pain of Musk repeatedly insisting that their transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, was “killed by the woke mind virus,” calling this an unconscionable comment given the actual loss of a child they experienced together. Musk goes on to tell Gibney that right after passing along the message that he would “always love” Wilson, he cut off their daughter’s health insurance and that he has “never tried to repair things” with her.

“He was constantly remarking on the ways he found me lacking,” Wilson says in recounting their marriage. She claims that when she reminded her husband that she was his spouse and not an employee, he told her, “If you were my employee, I would fire you.” Summing up their overall dynamic, she says: “I learned the term gaslighting through my relationship with Elon.”

St. Clair, defiantly outspoken against Musk since revealing in early 2025 that he had fathered a child with her, alleges that her whirlwind affair with the billionaire was a temporary illusion of compatibility that led to a messy and ongoing custody battle. (Musk also covers a custody dispute with Grimes that was eventually settled for undisclosed terms.) St. Clair says in the film that Musk lost interest in her once she was pregnant and claims that he sought to father children with other women. According to The Wall Street Journal, this included cryptocurrency influencer Tiffany Fong, whom he messaged with an offer to give her a child. (Musk did not immediately return a request for comment on this matter. Fong declined to comment publicly on the Journal’s story except to say that she had requested not to be included in the outlet’s reporting.)

“It’s like a Gatling gun of sperm in his DMs,” St. Clair quips. In the film’s interviews, both she and Wilson voice discomfort over their ex’s views on birth rates and ambition to father a “legion” of offspring, with Wilson claiming he regards the mothers of his children as replaceable “breeders.”

Elsewhere in the film, St. Clair covers her allegation that Musk retaliated against her by reducing his financial support for their son, Romulus. And her reluctance to touch on certain issues the filmmakers ask her about seems to serve as something of an answer in its own right. “I’m not at liberty to say,” she responds carefully when asked if she ever witnessed Musk using illegal drugs.

Gibney’s broad account of how Musk wove together a tech empire and his celebrity image through relentless self-mythologizing, then insulated it from government oversight by backing Trump and seizing power within his administration, is an utterly convincing one. But most of the story will be familiar to those who have kept up with Musk headlines for the past decade. What’s truly eye-opening in Musk is the way the women he was once close to talk about what they see as his boundless capacity for cruelty and narcissism.

Is there a world in which Zilis, too, comes forward to share her intimate conversations and correspondence with Musk? That surely depends on whether she has signed any legal documents like those presented to St. Clair. What’s more than evident, however, is that for all his resources, Musk can’t buy the silence of everyone he’s ever known, and if anyone can finally shred his aura of genius inventor-king, it’s the women he’s allowed—however briefly—to share his orbit.
